schools.summary: Gill reports the view that David had already repented privately and composed two penitential psalms before the visit.
Keil and Delitzsch give two reasons for the delay and read one of those psalms as describing the concealment rather than a completed repentance; Ellicott notes Nathan was already intimate with David.
Henry holds it certain that no psalms were penned in those nine months, and credits the prophet with two refusals.
Clarke declines to expound the parable and compares it to the letter Uriah carried; Wesley reads the timing as escalation after ordinary means failed.

debates.question: Had David repented privately before Nathan came?

sides.position: Some think so, having composed two penitential psalms before the visit, Nathan being sent to draw out a public repentance
He may have lamented in secret, but it is certain he penned no psalms in those nine months
One of those psalms describes not a completed repentance but the heart’s state while he concealed the crime

debates.question: Why did God wait so long?

sides.position: So that the fruit of the sin should first be brought to light, and the heart first broken by its own conscience
Because ordinary means had not awakened him, so God took an extraordinary course
Because God will not suffer his people to lie still in sin, and seeks us before we seek him

outliers.note: He declines to expound the parable at all, its bent being evident, and seals the point with a comparison: it was in David’s hand what his own letters had been in the hands of Uriah.

themes: a parable to draw out a sentence
1.pericope_label: Nathan comes to David: there were two men in one city

schools.summary: Gill enumerates David’s wives for the flocks and makes the lamb Uriah’s one wife, reporting Abarbinel on her age.
Henry allegorises the traveller and notices that the word changes to “husband” by the verse’s end.
Clarke finds the one detail in the story at variance with nature and fact; Wesley reads even the buying as having a counterpart.
Ellicott denies the parable is an allegory of David’s crimes at all, and admires its contrivance.

debates.question: Is the parable an allegory of David’s particular crimes?

sides.position: No: it alludes not to his special crimes but to the meanness and selfishness of the transaction
Yes, element by element: the flocks are his wives, the lamb Uriah’s wife, the traveller his lust

debates.question: Who or what is the traveller?

sides.position: Satan, a walker who is with good men only as a wayfaring man that does not abide
The evil imagination or concupiscence in the man himself
In David’s breast lust was but a wayfaring man tarrying a night, and did not dwell and rule there

outliers.note: He judges the lamb lying in the man’s bosom the only part of the parable at variance with nature and fact, treating the tale as an invention to be tested rather than a figure to be decoded.

2.pericope_label: The rich man had many flocks; the poor man had one little ewe lamb

schools.summary: Gill explains the vehemence by David’s taking the story for fact, and reports Kimchi and Weemse on an eightfold restitution.
Ellicott reads the anger as proof that his sense of justice survived; Keil and Delitzsch treat the parable as a trap that worked by not looking like one.
Henry imputes the severity to the roughness of a temper under guilt that had not yet received mercy.
Clarke notes the law did not sentence a sheep-stealer to death; Wesley reads the sentence as the injustice of a man indulgent to himself.

debates.question: What does David’s anger prove?

sides.position: That his generous impulses and warm sense of justice had survived his sin
The opposite: when most indulgent to himself he was most severe and even unjust to others
It must be imputed to the roughness of his temper, being under guilt and not yet having received mercy

debates.question: How much restitution was ordered?

sides.position: Fourfold, in exact accordance with the law
Eight lambs, the word being a dual, twice what the law commanded
holders: Kimchi and Weemse (as reported by Gill)

sides.position: Sevenfold in most Greek copies and fortyfold in the Chaldee, both expressing more of human indignation than of law

outliers.note: He points out that the law did not sentence a sheep-stealer to death at all, so that David passes the illegal penalty and the legal one in consecutive breaths.

5.pericope_label: David's anger: the man shall surely die, and restore fourfold

schools.summary: Gill supplies only the identification of the man meant.
Henry’s phrasing about the ambassador is what Wesley reproduces.
Clarke pushes the fourfold restitution into the history as four dead sons, and flags his own doubt about doing so.
Ellicott uses the shock as evidence that David was not essentially a bad man.

debates.question: Was the fourfold restitution paid in David’s own children?

sides.position: Perhaps: the child of Bathsheba, Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah all died untimely — though Clarke asks whether this indulges fancy too much

outliers.note: He argues that the conscience could not have been roused so had David been essentially a bad man: he was one whose main purpose was to do God’s will, stupefied by the delirium of prosperity and power.

themes: the fourfold debt paid in sons
7.pericope_label: Thou art the man: I anointed thee king over Israel

schools.summary: Gill rules out the palace at Gibeah and offers the household or the kingdom instead.
Henry widens the plural, counting Nabal among David’s former masters, and makes the bounty an aggravation of the sin.
Clarke takes the transfer as fact, explains it by custom, and shrugs off the objection he raises himself.
Ellicott doubts that David ever took Saul’s wives at all, the chronology forbidding it, and reads the clause as naming an entitlement.

debates.question: Did David actually take Saul’s wives?

sides.position: Yes, by the custom that a new king succeeded to his predecessor’s harem, possession being proof of regal right
Probably not: only one wife and one concubine are recorded, and the concubine was taken by Abner; the prophet names a right, not an inventory

outliers.note: He raises the incest objection himself — could David as Saul’s son-in-law take his father-in-law’s wives? — and answers that delicacy was seldom consulted in such cases.

8.pericope_label: I gave thee thy master's house, and would have given more

schools.summary: Gill names the sixth and seventh precepts as the commandment despised, and extends the sword past David’s life into his posterity.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree on the two verbs for the killing but limit the sentence by opposite routes.
Henry states the principle that those who despise God’s law despise God himself.
Clarke compresses the charge: thou art the murderer, the Ammonite sword thy instrument only.

debates.question: How long is “the sword shall never depart from thine house”?

sides.position: “For ever” keeps its literal force; what is limited is “thy house”, meaning his household until his death
The word means the longest time possible for its subject, and so here as long as David lives
It ran on past his death, in his posterity’s wars with Israel and other nations

outliers.note: They add an aggravation the others do not: the deed was done by the sword of the Ammonites, the enemies of the people of God.

themes: the sword of the children of Ammon
9.pericope_label: Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment of the LORD?

schools.summary: Gill prefaces the oracle by noting that Nathan spoke under a spirit of prophecy, and traces the stages of the concealment.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the twofold punishment answering a twofold sin, and note that the order is reversed.
Henry puts the correspondence in a figure and cites the customary retribution from Job.
Clarke and Wesley both convert the first-person threat into permissive providence.

debates.question: Is God the agent of what is threatened?

sides.position: It means that in the course of his providence he will permit it; David by his sin has made his friend his enemy
The words stand as God’s, whatever the agency; Nathan spoke under a spirit of prophecy

outliers.note: He holds that God expressed the threat darkly, naming neither agent nor manner, so that its accomplishment should not be hindered — the same reason Henry gives.

themes: evil out of thine own house
in the sight of this sun
11.pericope_label: I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house

schools.summary: Gill calls the four-word confession short but full, and cites the psalm as evidence of it.
Ellicott makes the promise of life an assurance of forgiveness and contrasts the confession with Saul’s; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the verb as forgiving and quote a comment on the brevity.
Henry reads the death escaped as eternal death, the obligation to punishment being cancelled.
Clarke denies that any pardon is granted here and builds a doctrine of transfer from the Hebrew; Wesley limits the remission to David’s own life.

debates.question: What does “thou shalt not die” remit?

sides.position: Not pardon at all, but reprieve from temporal death, to give time to repent and find mercy
The sin put away so far as concerns David’s own life
Forgiveness: the clause is parallel to and explanatory of the putting away of the sin
Not dying eternally, the obligation to punishment being cancelled — which is the nature of forgiveness

debates.question: What does the psalm of this occasion show?

sides.position: How full the brief confession was
That David had not yet received pardon when he wrote it, since in it he is still confessing in order to find mercy

outliers.note: He renders the verb as the LORD causing the sin to pass over, or transferring it, and takes the legal punishment to have been transferred to the child.

themes: I have sinned against the LORD
the sin caused to pass over
13.pericope_label: I have sinned against the LORD

schools.summary: Gill calls the deed a complicated wickedness, counting the adultery, the murder and the other deaths occasioned.
Henry supplies the blasphemers’ taunts and distinguishes between giving cause and giving colour for reproach.
Ellicott states a general principle, that natural consequences run their course however fully the sinner is forgiven.

debates.question: Why should a forgiven man be publicly punished?

sides.position: For the vindication of God’s justice and to destroy the hope that other sins might go unpunished; and because consequences flow on under the laws of moral government
To let the world see that though God loves David he hates his sin

debates.question: Is the death of one infant a light punishment?

sides.position: It might seem so in the harem of a great eastern monarch, but David saw it as evidence of an unalterable purpose
Infant deaths were perhaps rarer then, which would make it the more evident token of displeasure

outliers.note: He states the difficulty as plainly as it can be put — the guilty parent lives and the guiltless infant dies — and resolves it into sovereignty: the landlord may distrain upon any part of the premises he chooses.

14.pericope_label: The child that is born unto thee shall surely die

schools.summary: Gill has the prophet go home having nothing more from the LORD to say.
Keil and Delitzsch note only that the announced punishment was inflicted without delay.
Henry supposes Nathan went home to pray, and traces the honour done to his name in David’s later son.
Clarke reads the Hebrew as prescribing a seven-day dying rather than an immediate death.

debates.question: What did David do when the prophet left?

sides.position: He retired and composed the fifty-first psalm, praying for a pardon he had already been assured of

outliers.note: He treats the diseases and deaths of infants, who have not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, as sensible proofs of the original sin in which they are conceived.

15.pericope_label: The LORD struck the child, and it was very sick

schools.summary: Gill has David pray in the tabernacle he had built for the ark, and takes the threatening to be conditional.
Keil and Delitzsch rule out the sanctuary from what is said of his going up later; Ellicott moves the motive off the child and onto the sign.
Henry counts four marks of true repentance in the fasting and supplies the Hezekiah precedent.
Clarke denies the sentence could be reversed at all; Wesley traces the mourning to a sense of sin rather than fear of loss.

debates.question: Why pray after the sentence had been declared?

sides.position: Because the threatening might be conditional, as in the reprieve of Hezekiah
It could not be reversed: justice required the penalty of father or son
To avert the stroke as a sign of wrath, hoping to read in the child’s survival a proof of restored favour

debates.question: Where did David pray?

sides.position: In the tabernacle he had built for the ark
Not in the sanctuary, as his going up there afterwards shows, but in his own house or chamber

outliers.note: Having endorsed Otto von Gerlach’s reading that the prayer sprang from no excessive love of a created object, he adds a qualification of his own: David’s deep love for the child is not to be overlooked altogether.

themes: David besought God for the child
fasting and lying on the earth
why pray against a declared sentence
16.pericope_label: David fasted and lay all night upon the earth

schools.summary: Gill argues for the seventh day from birth on the ground that David cannot be thought to have fasted seven days.
Keil and Delitzsch give the servants’ reasoning and have David read the whispering before he asks.
Henry counts the same way as Gill and draws the consequence about circumcision.
Clarke and Wesley date the seventh day from the onset of the illness.

debates.question: Seventh day from what?

sides.position: From the child’s birth; David cannot be thought to have fasted seven days together
From the beginning of the distemper

outliers.note: On his reckoning the child died before the eighth day and so uncircumcised, which David might read as a further token of displeasure; yet Henry denies this put the child’s happiness in doubt, the covenant’s benefits not depending on its seals.

themes: on the seventh day the child died
the servants feared to tell him
18.pericope_label: The child died, and David perceived it

schools.summary: Gill notes only that he rose from the floor on which he lay.
Keil and Delitzsch list the three acts as the formal laying aside of mourning and identify the house of the LORD as the tent on Zion.
Henry justifies worship at such a moment by Job’s example and the maxim that weeping must not hinder worshipping.
Clarke supplies a comparative custom; Wesley itemises five purposes for the visit.

debates.question: What did David go to the sanctuary to do?

sides.position: To confess, own God’s justice, deprecate his displeasure, acknowledge the mercy that spared his life, and offer the required sacrifices
To acknowledge the hand of God, submit to his will, give thanks that he was spared, and pray that the controversy go no further

outliers.note: He notes that bathing, anointing the body and changing the apparel are the first outward signs among the Hindoos of coming out of mourning or sickness.

themes: came into the house of the LORD
20.pericope_label: He arose, washed, worshipped, and did eat

schools.summary: Gill observes that the servants knew what had been done and asked only after its meaning.
Henry turns the answer into a rule for praying without a particular promise to build on.
Clarke claims that all under the Mosaic dispensation held threatenings conditional, which sits oddly against his own earlier objection.

debates.question: Why did David importune while the child lived?

sides.position: Because all under that dispensation held God’s threatenings conditional and sought a change of purpose; this was the sole reason of his importunity
Because for all he knew the threatening might be conditional, and God gives leave to be earnest without a particular promise

outliers.note: His claim here that David sought a change of purpose because threatenings were held conditional is hard to square with his objection six verses earlier that the sentence could not be reversed.

themes: what thing is this that thou hast done
who can tell whether God will be gracious
while there is life there is hope
21.pericope_label: While the child was yet alive I fasted and wept

schools.summary: Gill makes the first half plain futility: to fast and pray now answers no end.
Keil and Delitzsch endorse Clericus’s bare paraphrase; Ellicott names that reading in order to refuse it.
Henry takes both senses, the grave and heaven, and draws hope for children dying in infancy.
Clarke separates what David meant from what is true, and fetches the consolation from Cicero as well as Scripture.

debates.question: What does “I shall go to him” mean?

sides.position: I shall go to the dead, the dead will not come to me
Not that Stoic sense: in David’s mouth it can scarcely be anything but confidence in conscious life beyond the grave and future recognition
It is not clear what David meant; it may mean only that he too will die — though the thing itself is true
Both: to him in the grave, and to him in heaven

outliers.note: He quotes at length a passage of Cicero in which Cato looks for the day he will join the company of souls gone before, and find there the son whose body he had laid on the pyre — to show that even the heathen drew comfort from expecting to meet their friends.

themes: can I bring him back again
a life of consciousness beyond the grave
23.pericope_label: I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me

schools.summary: Gill reconstructs Bathsheba’s distress, including a scruple whether it was lawful to go on living with David, and lays out three readings of the sending by Nathan.
Keil and Delitzsch make the name a pledge of peace with God and expressly deny the war derivation; Ellicott dates the birth after Rabbah and denies the second name was ever a title.
Henry reads the second name as doctrine, the covenant taking away all attainder of blood.
Clarke finds it strange that the father’s name prevailed, and blames the attachment for all David’s misfortunes; Wesley finds the closing clause ambiguous.

debates.question: Why was the child called Solomon?

sides.position: As a pledge that David was again a partaker of peace with God, and not from the Ammonite war being over
Prophetically, there having been almost unbroken peace throughout his reign
For all three reasons at once: peace with God, the prosperity entailed, and the type of the prince of peace

debates.question: Why did the name Jedidiah not stick?

sides.position: It is strange that the name given by the father was the one that prevailed
It was never meant as more than an expression of divine acceptance, and never came into use as a personal name

outliers.note: He suggests Bathsheba may have had a scruple whether it was lawful to go on living with David at all, and that the comfort offered her was the pardon of the iniquity and the promise of a son to succeed him.

24.pericope_label: Solomon born, and the LORD loved him

schools.summary: Gill explains the narrative order, the siege being finished earlier but reported here so the Bathsheba story might lie together.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both resolve the apparent contradiction by distinguishing the town from its citadel, and describe the ground.
Henry reads Joab’s message as honourable and marvels that the victory was granted before the repentance.
Clarke reports a reading that turns the city of waters into the cutting off of the city’s water; Wesley derives the name from the town being encompassed with water.

debates.question: How can Joab take the city and then ask David to take it?

sides.position: Rabbah comprised a city and a citadel: Joab took the former and sent for David before mastering the latter

debates.question: What made it the city of waters?

sides.position: The city held the tank or reservoir that supplied the town
The town was encompassed with water
The clause may mean not that he took the water-city but that he cut off the city’s waters
holders: Houbigant and Josephus (as reported by Clarke)

outliers.note: He pauses on the oddity of the victory: God might justly have made the Ammonite sword a standing plague to David, and instead gave him success before he repented, so that the goodness might lead him to repentance.

themes: lest it be called after my name
26.pericope_label: Joab fought against Rabbah and took the city of waters

schools.summary: Gill adds a purpose the others omit, the conquest of the other Ammonite cities and the carrying off of their spoil.
Ellicott offers two reasons for the muster and does not decide between them.
Wesley holds that no further strength was needed and reads the stated motive bluntly.

debates.question: Why muster the whole army for what remained?

sides.position: Either because more force was genuinely needed, or simply so that the formal capture should be David’s
No more force was needed: the rest could not long stand out, and the motive was the honour of taking it
Partly to recruit Joab’s weakened troops, partly to take the other Ammonite cities

themes: gather the rest of the people
lest the city be called after my name
28.pericope_label: Gather the rest of the people, lest the city be called after my name

schools.summary: Gill names the Ammonite king who had abused the ambassadors as the one stripped of his ensigns of royalty.
Keil and Delitzsch distrust the figure as an approximate estimate too high; Ellicott proposes a lighter eastern talent and dismisses the idol reading.
Clarke and Wesley both take the word as price rather than weight, arguing from the precious stones.

debates.question: How is the talent of gold to be understood?

sides.position: As an approximate estimate, somewhat too high, since no man could bear such a crown
As price and not weight, the precious stones never being valued by the weight of gold
As a lighter eastern talent, such as may have been current among the Ammonites
As Whiston’s talent of seven pounds, on which David might have carried it easily

outliers.note: He notes that the letters rendered “their king” would also spell the name of the chief Ammonite idol, and calls the supposition that the idol’s crown is meant quite unnecessary.

30.pericope_label: The crown of their king, a talent of gold

schools.summary: Gill limits the victims to the Ammonite princes who had advised the usage of the ambassadors.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both emend the single letter toward the harsher sense; Ellicott historicises David’s conduct rather than judging it.
Henry condemns the cruelty and reads it as a sign that David had not yet found mercy.
Clarke emends the same letter the other way and denies any torture; Wesley limits the victims and dates the cruelty to David’s impenitence.

debates.question: Does the verse describe torture or forced labour?

sides.position: Torture: the letter should be changed to agree with Chronicles, “he cut them with saws”
Forced labour: the milder word is the reading here, and even some Chronicles manuscripts carry it, so sawing and hewing human beings have no place in the text

debates.question: Who were put to death?

sides.position: Not all the inhabitants, but the princes who advised the abuse of the ambassadors and those who approved it
The word is indefinite, and means the men of war and chiefly the authors of that usage
The inhabitants, and with cruel tortures

debates.question: How is David’s conduct to be judged?

sides.position: Extremely rigorous, and a sign his heart was not yet made soft by repentance
Done while his heart was hardened and he was bereaved of the Spirit that would have taught him mercy
Neither excused nor condemned: he acted by the customs and knowledge of his time, without suspecting they were not God’s will

outliers.note: He adopts the marginal reading of the last clause, making it the furnace of Molech, and finds the justice of it — they were punished with their own sin and with the punishment they had inflicted on their children.

themes: the brick-kiln or the furnace of Molech
31.pericope_label: He brought forth the people and put them under saws
